#3251. Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The partnership could provide one of the nation’s largest AI companies with a bevy of personal medical data.

A major US healthcare technology provider just teamed up with Anthropic to connect patient health records with Claude.

Athenahealth, a healthcare technology provider serving over 20% of the US population, launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) compatible server that connects to Anthropic’s Claude. The server, named AthenaPatient MCP, allows the AI model to gather information from health records and answer related questions. The process is secure, according to Athenahealth, and requires patients to sign in with their account credentials.

AthenaPatient MCP is available only to Claude Pro and Claude Max users, which cost $20 and $100 per month, respectively. Not all Athenahealth patients will have their data shared with Claude, and not all Claude Pro and Claude Max users must opt in. Users must give Claude their authenticated Athenahealth credentials, can choose which health information Claude can access, and can revoke access at any time, according to the press release.

Also: The wearable health boom is creating a data overload for doctors – what happens next

Once authorized, Claude takes patients’ information like lab results, vitals, medications, health conditions, immunizations, visit history, diagnostic reports, allergies, procedures, and care plans into account when answering questions.

The AI partnership does not provide medical advice, according to Sam Lambson, vice president of product management, data & ecosystem at Athenahealth, who responded to ZDNET in an email. It also should not replace a clinician’s professional judgment or medical advice. “Patients should contact a qualified healthcare professional with questions about diagnosis, treatment, or changes to their care,” Lambson said.

It appears that the AthenaPatient MCP tool is designed to help patients better understand the information provided by health professionals, rather than to give them medical advice. So, one may ask AthenaPatient MCP about their latest blood test results, such as “What was my most recent red blood cell count?” but users shouldn’t expect Claude to explain how an abnormally high or low count may affect them.

Athenahealth says that the agreement prohibits Anthropic from using data accessed through this connection to train its models or improve its products.

Partnerships between big tech and big healthcare aren’t new. In fact, the collaboration between Athenahealth and Anthropic follows a larger trend across the health tech industry. Earlier this year, Microsoft teamed up with Mayo Clinic to develop an AI model for healthcare; Boston Children’s Hospital forged a partnership with OpenAI to develop an enterprise AI system for use across research, clinical, and administrative teams, according to a press release.

Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

A growing number of Americans are consulting AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. This partnership makes the process slightly more secure by authorizing patient account credentials before granting the model access to health records.

Health data is extremely valuable, and tech companies are increasingly interested in partnering with healthcare providers to access it. Much of the “AI could cure cancer” messaging we hear relies on these humongous companies obtaining enough health data to train their AI models and link disease data to patient data. This is not to say, however, that solving this complex issue is the motive behind the partnership between Athenahealth and Anthropic.

Also: Asking AI for medical advice? There’s a right and wrong way, one doctor explains

A more reasonable explanation for such a partnership is that an AI that can answer patient queries could eliminate some of the admin work doctors do between patient visits, like answering questions about test results, giving Athenahealth doctors some time back.

Will partnerships like Anthropic and Athenahealth’s improve patient outcomes? That remains to be seen, but a recent survey by Pew Research Center found that Americans aren’t that confident on the matter. The largest shares of respondents still preferred that a human oversee AI when it’s used in a clinical context.

#3248. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

#3246. Here's How Many Shares of McDonald's You'd Need for $2,000 in Yearly Dividends

It may be worth waiting for McDonald's to show improvement in its U.S. store sales before buying the stock.

McDonald's (MCD -0.78%) is fresh off reporting its 2026 third-quarter results. While it was a mixed bag, the stock price climbed over 5% by the afternoon of the report, suggesting the markets were somewhat pleased.

The company reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. locations open for at least 13 months and missed CNBC-tracked analyst estimates of $7.2 billion in revenue, reporting $7.1 billion. McDonald's did, however, beat earnings per share (EPS) estimates of $3.38, reporting EPS of $3.57. It also reported net income of $2.4 billion, an increase from $2.2 billion in the prior-year period.

For any investor who likes the results and sees McDonald's as an investment candidate, or for a current shareholder thinking about picking up more shares, a bonus of owning the stock is that it pays a dividend. It yields a respectable 2.7%, so we can run through a hypothetical example of how many shares it would take to generate $2,000 a year in dividend payouts.

With a quarterly dividend payout of $1.93, it would require about 260 shares of McDonald's to receive $500 per quarter, totaling a yearly dividend of $2,000.

With an opening price of $268.79 on Nov. 4, acquiring those 260 shares would cost around $69,885.

Small investments can compound over time, so even if only a handful of shares are purchased initially, they can add up. That said, I would still feel comfortable sitting on the sidelines and waiting to invest in McDonald's. Also: This 15-inch portable monitor solved my big issue with cheaper models – and rivals my Mac display

Everything, and I mean everything, about this phone is fast.

Since the RedMagic 12 Pro is advertised as a serious gaming phone, why does it include preinstalled games that are decidedly non-serious?

Either way, the RedMagic 12 Pro is a phone that belongs at the top of the heap among flagships, even above every Pixel phone ever released. If there is a phone that can impress me more than the RedMagic 12 Pro, I’ve yet to see it.

#3239. Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.

#3238. Bread as a Sponge for Oil Is the Best Kitchen Hack I Learned All Year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Oily pans, stews and sauces are no match for the bread sponge trick.

If you want to degrease a pan or the top layer of an oily sauce without ruining a sponge, a single slice of bread could be your new favorite cleaning sidekick.

While we have vastly improved how we dispose of most things, excess cooking grease still presents a problem. Down the sink? Not advisable. Neither is the dishwasher—even the garbage bin can become a gnarly affair.

Getting the bulk of the grease out of a pan after cooking a batch of bacon or burgers is a good first step, but that greasy pan will either take down a sponge or half a roll of paper towels. What if a humble slice of past-its-prime sandwich bread was the all-natural solution for greasy pans you’ve been looking for?

It’s cheap and easy, and you can toss the used-up bread into a compost bin or countertop food waste processor without disrupting its yuck-free operation.

So, is it ever OK to pour excess grease or used cooking oil down the sink? Even if you run the hot water tap at the same time? Short answer: no. Long answer? Here’s an expert for the “no.” “When grease cools, it solidifies, coating the interior of the pipe,” says Jacylyn Basilone, chief operating officer of Brooks Plumbing. Even if you’re running hot water, the grease will eventually cool further down the line and cause future problems. “Over time, the solidified grease in the pipes can catch debris, thus making a partial clog grow larger and larger,” she says, reducing the pipe’s circumference little by little if you do this repeatedly.

Unlike a clogged shower drain, which you can usually clear easily, “a normal sewer machine or ‘snake’ can’t alleviate this type of stoppage,” says Basilone. “While grease solidifies, it can’t be captured by the claw head. Grease removal is best remediated with a hydrojetter, which tends to be more expensive than the traditional drain-cleaning services.”

Bread is the real answer, and I can’t believe I haven’t been doing this all along. (*Hangs head in shame, fully guilty of relying on the obviously very sketchy hot water method.*)

Bread has always been a superb grease-mopping tool; we usually think of it in a culinary context rather than for waste removal. Just as you’d drag a crusty baguette or hunk of ciabatta across the drippings on your plate, bread is an excellent sponge for all manner of oil, whether or not it is appealing to consume. Using bread to soak up excess oil essentially turns liquid food waste into a solid, making disposal much easier.

If it’s not obvious, this is also a great way to use bread that might otherwise go to waste: the ends of the loaf you can’t bring yourself to eat, or bread that’s gone stale or is starting to show the first mold spores. If you’re going to discard the bread anyway, at least put it to good use.

The bread trick comes in handy in almost endless ways. If there’s a pool of oil, it’s the mop for the job. I initially tried it after cooking bacon. A single, small slice of bread was enough to absorb what was easily four to six ounces of liquid grease left in the pan. I dragged the slice around the pan like a mop, but even after letting it sit a few extra moments, it kept working and eventually soaked up all the liquid grease. (If you’re feeling indulgent and used a fresh bread slice for this purpose, the temptation to make pretty epic croutons here is quite strong — another upside.)

If your air fryer has space between the drawer and the basket, you can place the bread there to soak up grease while cooking. Even for oily, slow-cooked proteins like pork shoulder, you can press the bread onto the meat to soak up grease before serving.

Once the bread has absorbed the oil and needs discarding, responsible food-waste methods are much easier to manage. Depending on how much oil the bread has absorbed, you can safely put the soaked bread in the compost bin or countertop composter without risking a major oil spill and a mess to clean up later. Oil can slow decomposition, so composting large amounts isn’t recommended. Small amounts, such as a few tablespoons at a time, are safe.

Even if you have no other option but to throw it away — and if that is the case, please consider getting a small composting appliance — at the very least, you’re not involving an easily recyclable glass container.

#3236. How To Build Real AI Sovereignty

Antoni Kozelski, CEO/founder of Vstorm, an agentic AI engineering firm helping companies implement agentic AI to transform their businesses.

​Gartner forecasts that worldwide sovereign cloud spending will reach $80 billion in 2026, growing more than 35% from 2025. And yet the European Commission reports that the EU still depends on non-EU providers for over 80% of its key digital products, services and infrastructure. Money is pouring into the word “sovereign.” The dependence it is meant to fix has barely moved.

In my own work, I’ve found the reason is rarely the data center. It is ownership: which layers of the stack a company actually holds, which it rents and who can revoke them. Nearly every client who asks us for a “sovereign” system means something different by the word.

The instinct to treat sovereignty as a location (e.g., “Our data sits in-country, and therefore, we are sovereign.”) is the first and most expensive mistake leaders can make. Location is not control. The CLOUD Act lets U.S. authorities compel a U.S.-incorporated provider to hand over data held anywhere in the world, including in an EU data center. The postcode on the server changes nothing. What governs the system is the law that governs the company operating it.

Jurisdiction follows the company, not the data center. Data residency asks where information sits. AI sovereignty asks who holds legal and operational authority over it and whether a foreign entity could alter, disable or disclose it without consent.

No one has finished writing the rules yet. The EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act is still moving through negotiation, its sovereignty framework unsettled. Open standards for agentic systems are still being drafted; the Agentic AI Foundation, hosted by the Linux Foundation and launched in late 2025, exists to coordinate those standards, and my company contributes to that work.

When the standards are still forming, every architecture decision is a sovereignty decision, whether a team recognizes it or not.

I have worked with many organizations that believed they had bought sovereignty, but in reality, they had not. The failure modes I’ve observed are strikingly similar each time:

1. They treat data residency as sovereignty. A local region and a national label are often mistaken for control, but if the control plane, the billing or the support team answers to a foreign parent, the data is still reachable. This is what the industry now calls sovereignty washing.

2. They rent the intelligence layer without noticing. A company can own its prompts, its data and even its process logic and still not own the codebase the system runs on, paying indefinitely for the one layer that decides what the system is allowed to do.

3. They confuse model access with ownership. The models are available to everyone. Calling a closed model through an API is not the same as holding open weights you can run, move or swap on infrastructure you control.

4. They leave the exit untested. The real proof of ownership is whether you can leave. If taking your data and your logic to another provider means a rebuild, you did not own them; you were renting them all along.

Sovereignty is a spectrum, not a switch, and it’s a mistake to chase all of it at once. No single company controls the whole stack—the chips and the critical minerals beneath them are transnational and out of anyone’s sole reach. Real returns come from sequencing, not scale: Own the layers that would hurt most to lose, prove you can exit and then decide what to rent deliberately.

The order is simple: Start with the layers whose loss would cost the most: your data and the process logic that encodes how you run. Next, prove you can move before you scale. Export the data, swap the model and change the provider without re-architecting. Finally, own the deepest layers you reasonably can and rent the rest as a choice, not a default.​

Across the sovereign systems that hold up, I’ve seen three common traits:

1. They are portable. Providers, models and infrastructure can change without a rebuild, but portability is the working test of agentic AI without vendor lock-in.

2. Jurisdiction sits with an entity the owner controls, not a foreign parent that can be compelled from outside.

3. The code and the process logic are held, not licensed indefinitely.

The cost of getting this wrong is now measurable. The Commission’s own target is to cut “EU reliance on non-EU technology providers from more than 80 percent today to 40 percent by 2030,” an admission of how deep the exposure runs. Under the EU AI Act, data-governance failures on high-risk systems carry fines up to €35 million or up to 7% of annual worldwide turnover. And there is a physical floor: The IEA projects data centers will draw around 1,000 TWh by 2030, roughly Japan’s entire electricity consumption. A system you cannot power is sovereign in name only.

The “sovereign” label is a commodity. What decides true sovereignty is which layers you actually own. Again, sovereignty is not the postcode on the server. It is the deed to the house.​​

#3235. Scientists Build Biocomputer That Runs on Bacteria to Solve Hard Problems

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The study relied on the bacterium E. coli and V. natriegens to run the calculations.

Move over, microchips. The next generation of supercomputing might just run on living bacteria. For 20 years, an international team of scientists has been developing a biocomputer that uses bacteria to process information. Scientists from McGill University in Montreal announced their findings on Nov. 3 and published a paper detailing the results earlier this year in Nature.

Researchers from Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom and Australia contributed to this work, which combines biology with computer science and engineering. The researchers say the resulting biocomputer could be used to solve problems that give standard computers a hard time.

“Electronic (sequential) computers are not meant, or designed, to solve decision trees,” Dan Nicolau, a McGill bioengineering professor and senior author for the research paper, told CNET via email.

Nicolau noted that if electronic computers are to solve these types of problems, the computers will need a lot of RAM.

The study relied on the bacterium Escherichia coli and Vibrio natriegens to run the calculations. The researchers used E. coli because it moves through fluid in a predictable, measurable way and V. natriegens because it reproduces very quickly.

By using live bacteria rather than digital processing, the team says the biocomputer can solve big, complex problems at a small fraction of the memory and resources that regular computers require.

The researchers tested the biocomputer with a seemingly simple math problem called the Subset Sum Problem, which famously becomes exponentially harder as the number of inputs increases.

When the Subset Sum Problem inputs grow too large, the problem is known to give traditional computers issues, such as taking centuries, or even millions of years, to solve the problem.

The researchers translated the problem into a graph that branches off into each possible combination of inputs. Next, the team created a tiny physical structure that mirrored the Subset Sum Problem graph.

Inside the structure, they built a network of tunnels to mirror the graph branches. Each fork in the tunnels represents a decision point, and every possible route through the tunnels represents a different solution to the problem.

The researchers unleashed bacteria, which rapidly reproduce, inside the tunnels. The fast-growing bacteria moved through the tunnels, exploring many routes to the solution simultaneously.

Compared to digital processing, the bacteria are slow. But rather than tackling a problem sequentially, as traditional computers do, the bacteria can examine many solutions at once. And if you need more computing power, bacterial reproduction within the tunnels creates additional processing units to help solve the problem.

The team used automated image analysis to follow the bacteria through the correct tunnels. In this way, the researchers were able to tell which paths through the network satisfied the problem’s constraints.

The researchers were also able to adjust temperatures to prevent bacteria overcrowding while traveling through the network.

Enterprising fans have figured out how to run Doom, the groundbreaking 1993 first-person shooter video game, on everything from E. coli to a thermostat. Nicolau says Doom could probably run on the new system, with an important caveat concerning the biocomputer’s size.

“(The biocomputer) must be huge!” Nicolau said. Because bacteria make slow processors, you would need a massive biocomputer to host enough bacteria to run a video game.

But because no RAM is needed, Nicolau said biocomputing could help to solve the global RAM shortage, and even broaden our understanding of what a computer could be.

“A computer is a device which accepts (input) numbers and gets out (output) numbers. Full stop,” he said. “All other uses of the word computer (are) from our point of view, well, poetical.”

#3234. This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You won't see the 'suspended' sign because it's not meant for you.

KELA researchers have exposed an active financial-scam infrastructure that hosts hundreds of fraudulent websites capable of faking their own suspensions to stay online. As of Oct. 25, 2026, 248 financial scam and phishing domains tied to 189 major US banks and financial services have been linked to the same infrastructure.

According to the cybersecurity firm’s report, published on Tuesday, the “Suspended” infrastructure operation runs websites that have cloned the official domains of victim organizations, with a particular focus on business banking. Many domains use the [keyword]-[bank].com format, slotting in keywords such as “secure,” “disable,” “protect,” and “cancel.”

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

A handful of servers spread across two shared hosting providers run the backend of Suspended infrastructure, which has also been tied to phishing campaigns targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and government services in the UK, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand. As a result, the researchers believe that either a single operator is behind the setup or that the server infrastructure is part of a wider phishing-as-a-service platform.

This phishing campaign stands out because of how the cybercriminals behind the scam are protecting it: by issuing takedown notices.

When you visit a website and see a message that it has been taken down or suspended, it’s usually because the domain has been associated with malicious or illegal activity, including phishing and scams. Law enforcement agencies, often with help from technology firms, find these websites, obtain the necessary court orders, and seize the infrastructure or accounts behind them to force a suspension through a registrar or hosting provider.

You see the notice, you move on — and this also goes for scanners and security teams.

However, in this case, the scam artists created a mechanism to show it themselves, to avoid being flagged and taken down. But it’s when they show it that matters.

The false suspension notice appears deceptively simple at first glance. A phishing kit embedded in the domain registers the IP address of each visitor, and on their second visit, they are shown a fake “account suspended” page. The kit is disguised as a challenge page similar to those legitimately used by Cloudflare.

Researchers also detected other decoys, including “Sorry, you’ve been blocked” notices, blank pages, and redirections to Google. Some pages also have reCAPTCHAs, and the researchers detected scripts that block browser developer tools, likely to slow analysis.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how

But why show fake suspension notices in the first place? To scanners and cybersecurity teams, it looks like someone else has already dealt with the malicious domain, and they can move on to the next suspicious website.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down,” KELA says. “A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team or a takedown provider checks a reported site and then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown.”

As shown in the image below, while scanners would detect a suspension notice, victims would still see the cloned website, complete with lures to entice them into entering their information, leading to financial fraud and potentially identity theft. After all, one visit is enough.

As of this writing, there are 248 live domains, plus those taken offline after the researchers disclosed their findings to law enforcement; over 300 scam domains have been hosted on the same infrastructure since May this year. Unfortunately, this phishing campaign remains active, with new domains appearing every day.

One lead could reveal the operator: a remote desktop connection to the malicious infrastructure through a standard UK home broadband connection, but it has not been verified.

Use a phishing link checker to verify whether a URL is trustworthy, and remember that any email or message claiming to be from your bank may be fraudulent.

When it comes to organizations, KELA has released a free Bank Phishing Check tool that compares official domains and organizations against the websites uncovered during the firm’s research.

#3233. How These 5 Bond ETFs Differ and When Each One Fits

A guide to matching the bond ETF to the job it will perform in your portfolio.

Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF (BND +0.21%), iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF (NYSEMKET: AGG), Vanguard Short-Term Treasury ETF (VGSH +0.23%), iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT +0.21%), and Vanguard Total International Bond ETF (BNDX +0.15%) rank among the largest bond ETFs. While they might all look similar at first glance, these funds can be quite different.

Here's a look at what you need to know about these top bond ETFs and when each one would fit in a portfolio.

The Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF and iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF rank as the two largest bond ETFs by assets under management (AUM) at $167 billion and $139 billion, respectively. They both aim to provide broad exposure to the total U.S. bond market for investors seeking income and diversification. Here's how these two top bond ETFs compare:

As the table shows, these are very similar funds (they also share the same 0.03% expense ratio). BND provides investors with a slightly higher yield, while AGG holds more bonds. There are a few other subtle differences in their holdings (AGG has higher exposure to MBS, while BND has higher exposure to AAA-rated bonds).

Overall, the differences are so subtle that either fund would be an ideal core bond holding. You'd probably only hold one of these ETFs, with the choice likely coming down to sponsor preference (Vanguard or BlackRock).

Whereas BND and AGG are close cousins, the Vanguard Short-Term Treasury ETF and iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF are opposites. VGSH primarily invests in short-term U.S. Treasury bonds (one- to three-year maturities), while TLT invests in long-duration U.S. government debt (20+ years). That makes a huge difference in returns and volatility.

VGSH offers current income with modest price fluctuations, while TLT offers higher income potential but greater volatility. The big difference is duration, which measures the sensitivity of bond ETF prices to interest rate movements. For example, if a bond ETF has a duration of two years, its price would fall about 2% when interest rates rise 1 percentage point, while rising 2% if rates fall by 1 percentage point. The higher the duration, the greater the price movement when interest rates change. VGSH's average duration is 1.9 years compared to 14.9 years for TLT. So, you'd want to buy VGSH for stability, and TLT if you expect interest rates to fall.

Vanguard Total International Bond ETF provides broad exposure to major bond markets outside the U.S. It employs hedging strategies to mitigate foreign-currency risk. The ETF currently holds 6,837 bonds from across the world. Most of its bonds have investment-grade ratings, with 79% issued by foreign governments. Its portfolio has a 5.5% yield to maturity and a 6.4-year average duration. In many ways, it would be similar to owning BND or AGG, though with a bit more rate sensitivity. This ETF would be ideal for investors seeking to further diversify their bond portfolio with some international exposure. It would be a good long-term holding to complement either BND or AGG.

Bond ETFs are lower-risk investments compared to stocks. However, they're not risk-free investments. The biggest risk is duration. If interest rates rise, bond ETFs with high average durations would see price declines that could more than offset the income they provide. We can see that in the price changes of TLT versus the other bond ETFs over the past year:

Investors need to consider this risk before adding a longer-duration bond ETF to their portfolios.

Before choosing a bond ETF, ask what job you want the investment to accomplish for your portfolio. BND and AGG are best for core bond holdings. Meanwhile, VGSH is best for money you may need soon. TLT and BNDX have more specialized jobs. BNDX provides international diversification, while TLT is a bet on falling interest rates. The key is to make sure the bond ETF aligns with the role you expect it to play in your portfolio.

Experts explain how this hidden iPhone setting can improve your sleep

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I write about sleep for a living, but I've been secretly locked in a losing battle against my doomscrolling habits. I'd constantly push bedtime later to watch a few more reels or reply to a couple more messages — and my nocturnal phone habit meant that getting out of bed each morning was becoming a chore.

That was until I stumbled on a hidden feature in my Apple Health App. Now I'm far more disciplined when it comes to using my phone around bedtime, making a conscious effort to give myself time to truly relax in the evening and time to ease into the day come morning.

Below, I dig into how I altered my iPhone settings to help me get to sleep on time and wake up with tons more energy. Plus, Dr. Shelby Harris, a board-certified behavioral sleep medicine specialist and psychologist, explains why enabling this feature works and why it's so important to restrict phone use around bedtime for better sleep.

During my time as a sleep tech tester, I've tried my fair share of sleep gadgets. I'll forever rave about the top-rated sunrise alarm clocks and don't know where I'd be without by trusty Oura Ring to help track my rest. But, understandably, I'm yet to find anything that can physically restrain me from using my phone in bed.

"The biggest problem with your phone at night isn’t the screen itself," explains Dr. Harris, who has over 20 years' experience in sleep medicine. "It’s what’s on it. Social media, videos, and games are designed to keep you hooked, with endless feeds and autoplay that make it easy to lose track of time. Before you know it, “just a few minutes” has turned into an hour of lost sleep."

Our willpower is no match for Meta, basically. That's why it's so important nowadays to have measures and discipline in place to stop the endless scrolling when you should be sleeping.

I recommend everybody turns on Sleep Schedule in the Apple Health app. This feature allows you to set a recurring bedtime and wake-up routine. During sleep time, your phone will automatically shift into Sleep Focus mode where notifications and calls are silenced, your lock screen simplifies and phone screens dims.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Without your phone constantly buzzing at your bedside, it's less tempting to pick up and even gives you the chance to forget about your constant notification feed while you drift off to sleep.

Depending on the Wind Down period you set, you'll get a notification telling you to prioritise your sleep. I get this 15 minutes before my desired bedtime, though I'm keen to push this earlier after hearing Dr. Harris' advice.

The Diplomate in Behavioral Sleep Medicine says: "The best approach is to put your phone away, ideally outside the bedroom, 30 to 60 minutes before bed and replace scrolling with something calming, like reading a book or stretching."

"The iPhone’s sleep tools help turn good intentions into habits," says Dr. Harris. To set up your personalised sleep schedule, head to the Apple Health app (that pink heart in a white square). Find the Sleep section and scroll down to 'Your Schedule'. Open 'Full Schedule & Options'.

Here you can toggle on Sleep Schedule and link it to your phone's Sleep Focus setting.

There's the option to customise your schedule for different days of the week. However, experts recommend sticking to the same sleep and wake times seven nights a week as this helps sync your circadian rhythm (more on this below).

You can also set a Wind Down period between 15 minutes and three hours. During this time, your phone shifts into Sleep mode. Health will notify you when Wind Down begins, encouraging you to transition from scrolling to rest.

For full peace of mind if you have caring responsibilities, you can select certain contacts to break through the notification block. This means you won't block out any important phone calls through the night.

Sleeping at consistent times from night to night is quickly becoming the most common sleep advice dished out by experts.

Recent science – including a major study by Vitality Research Institute – indicates the 7:1 sleep rule is the bedrock of quality rest. The rule stipulates getting seven hours of sleep every single night keeping your bedtime within in a one hour window is the secret to sleeping well, waking up energized, and indeed living up to four years longer.

Dr. Harris, who specialises in circadian rhythm disorders, explains: "Your body runs on an internal clock that controls when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert. When you go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, that clock learns to anticipate sleep, so you fall asleep faster, sleep more deeply, and wake up feeling more refreshed."

Sticking to a consistent sleep schedule helps sync your circadian rhythm. When this is in tune, your body will naturally release sleep-inducing hormones like melatonin around bedtime and suppress them come morning so you wake up without lingering grogginess (scientifically named sleep inertia).

Whereas "Irregular schedules, especially sleeping in on weekends, throw that rhythm off and leave you feeling jet-lagged without ever leaving home," adds Dr. Harris.

With a well regulated circadian cycle, you should release the right amount of melatonin through the night to keep you in a healthy sleep cycle, so you get good quality sleep and wake up feeling refreshed.

As your circadian rhythm also controls hormones that promote alertness (cortisol and serotonin), you should also experience more stable energy levels through the day.

Ultimately, the New York-based sleep psychologist advises, "If you focus on one thing, make it a consistent wake-up time. That’s the anchor that keeps everything else on track" — and Apple's Sleep Schedule feature can help you do just that, especially if you're a stickler for late night scrolling.

A two-in-one sunrise alarm clock and sleep tracker, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the ultimate gadget for keeping your sleep in check. Sunrise and sunset simulations help sync your body clock while gentle sounds lull you in and out of sleep – all for $249.99 plus a $4.99/month subscription fee to access all features.

Vetted the best sleep tracker around by our sleep tech reviewers, the Oura Ring 5 keeps track of the exact time you fall asleep and wake up, and helps coach you towards a consistent schedule. There's six colorways from gold to rose gold and silver and eight sizing options. Prices range from $399 to $499.

If it's a snoring partner getting in the way of your consistent sleep routine, the Loop Queit 2 Ear Plugs are a dream. Sitting subtly in your ears, they muffle sound without causing discomfort. Our reviewer, a chronically light sleeper, says: "The Loop Quiet 2 are ideal for dropping of peacefully without you missing your alarm in the morning." Prices start at $24.95 and they can be reused night after night.

#3231. Data Center Backers Suffer Near-Total Midterm Defeats Across the Country

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

More than 40 voting initiatives yielded almost nothing but resistance to data-center projects.

The 2026 midterm election blue wave, which shifted the balance of power in Congress and across state races toward Democrats, can be seen as a repudiation of AI and the controversial data centers that provide its computing power. Data center proponents have heavily backed President Donald Trump and Republican candidates, underscored by xAI CEO Elon Musk investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Texas midterm campaigns to support the industry.

But in many parts of the country, voters didn’t need to make their voices on data centers heard through candidates. They had direct initiatives on the ballot this week that would decide whether data center projects would move ahead in their districts.

In line with a growing backlash against data centers and AI, voters supported about 40 election-day measures that would restrict the construction of new data centers, with only one result — in Harwood, North Dakota — favoring data center expansion.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

As broken down by the website Data Centers on the Ballot, Ohio had the most number of voting measures: 21, all of which were in favor of restrictions.

Maine, Illinois, Kansas, New Jersey, California, Florida, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin were the other states with data center voting.

Six elections were held earlier in 2026 in California, Michigan, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, with all of them finding voters opposed to allowing data center builds to continue without new restrictions.

Not all the proposed restrictions were the same. In some elections, voters decided whether to impose a megawatt cap on data center energy use, while other measures addressed specific zoning issues or whether data center projects should require voter approval. Some proposed an outright ban on new data centers, and six of those were successful.

Polls by groups including Pew Research have found Americans have soured on data centers due to high electricity bills, water use and environmental concerns, among other reasons. It’s also hard to separate concerns about data centers from concerns about AI affecting jobs. AI has also become a divisive enough issue to affect midterm voting.

The election results were so bad for the industry that Politico declared data centers to be “the midterms’ other big loser” next to Republicans. Not only did voters enact additional restrictions on builds across the country, but data centers were mentioned in Democratic victory speeches.

“I do not work for data centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you, I work for Ohio,” Senator-elect Sherrod Brown said in his victory speech Tuesday night.

USA Today reported that two mayors, one in Oklahoma and one in Ohio, were recalled after public backlash over proposed data centers.

The midterms might have longer-term effects for tech companies and data center firms. It’s likely that with Democratic control of Congress, there’ll be more scrutiny.

“Public policy is going to reflect public opinion, and there’s been a very substantial change in public opinion just over the last year,” Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Politico.

Political headwinds from the midterms could lead local officials across the country to gain public favor by delaying or canceling data center projects or putting pressure on the companies behind them to offer more attractive deals to communities. The days of huge tax breaks and incentives for data centers could be coming to a close.

“Now, (communities) are pushing data centers to pay taxes, create their own power plants, pay for their use of electricity and water and contribute to local community resources like education funds,” The New York Times reported.

#3227. Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

#3226. AI Can Get Smarter Without Getting More Authority

Kognitos Founder & CEO Binny Gill holds nearly 100 patents in computer science.

​We all saw something unusual happen in AI as some of the people building the world’s most capable systems began arguing that the technology may be advancing faster than our ability to control it.​

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the industry to “pace the frontier,” warning that AI capabilities could advance faster than our ability to control them. Other AI leaders echoed this, and Anthropic began measuring how much AI contributes to developing future AI systems.​

I take those concerns seriously, but I think they also expose an assumption that deserves more scrutiny. We often talk as though greater intelligence must inevitably bring greater autonomy, when the two are separate engineering decisions.​

Traditionally, software has been created to perform a task and given the access needed to do it. With generative AI, the software can now determine what it thinks should happen next. An AI system can interpret a request, identify a problem and propose a course of action without that sequence having been explicitly programmed.

That capability does not require unrestricted authority to carry the proposal out.​

We understand this easily when dealing with people. A talented financial analyst may identify a multimillion-dollar opportunity, but that does not give the analyst permission to move the money. Organizations separate expertise from authority because knowing what should happen is different from having permission to do it.

Much of the frontier safety debate focuses on models themselves. Researchers want to understand model behavior and whether systems continue to follow human intent as their capabilities increase. But control can sit where the model’s reasoning meets the outside world.

Imagine an AI model concludes that a customer should receive a $20,000 refund. Whether that refund actually happens isn’t the model’s call. The business defines the rules: Refunds under $500 are issued automatically, anything over $5,000 requires a manager’s approval, and some actions are never permitted without a human. So the model recommends, and the execution layer applies those rules and routes this one for sign-off.

This is the value of keeping the execution layer deterministic. Generative AI reasons probabilistically; that’s inherent to how it works. But the rules governing what it can do can be explicit, predictable and enforceable.​

If someone has to click “approve” 10,000 times a day, we have re-created manual work under a different name. Keeping people in control is less about making humans approve everything and more about making humans responsible for the boundaries.​

Low-risk actions might execute automatically, while changes involving money, sensitive data or binding customer commitments require approval. Some operations may remain completely outside the AI system’s permissions.

Businesses already work this way. They establish permissions, approval thresholds, SOPs and separation of duties, then build systems that enforce them consistently.

AI needs an equivalent approach to authority. For an enterprise deploying agents, this produces much more useful questions than whether a model can simply be “trusted.” What can it change? When does somebody need to intervene? If something goes wrong six months from now, can we reconstruct what the model proposed, what rules applied and why an action was permitted?​

As models become more capable, it is tempting to give them broader access because additional permission makes the system appear more useful. The danger is that authority expands almost accidentally, one integration and one exception at a time.​

A model that becomes much better at reasoning may eventually reach conclusions that its users cannot easily follow. That creates a genuine interpretability challenge, but it does not follow that the same system must also be free to act on those conclusions without constraint.​

Remaining in control does not require people to stay more intelligent than the AI systems they use; it requires organizations to decide where those systems’ authority begins and ends.​

None of this removes AI risk. People can define bad policies, permissions can be misconfigured, and humans can approve the wrong action. But those failures happen at identifiable boundaries within the systems that can be tested, audited and improved.​

The recent Hugging Face incident is a good example; in this case, the guardrails didn’t fail the way people expected. The team believed the permissions were tight enough, and they were in testing. What broke them was the agent inventing a sequence of steps at runtime that nobody anticipated. This is a flaw in controlling an agent only through access: A sufficiently capable model will find a path through whatever access it has, and no permission set can enumerate every path in advance. ​

I favor separating planning from execution. A neurosymbolic architecture lets the model do what it is good at: reasoning about an ambiguous goal and producing a plan in plain English that a human can read and approve, then handing that plan to a symbolic engine that executes it exactly as written. The model cannot improvise new steps at runtime because it is no longer the thing running.

Over time, approved plans become a library of safe building blocks the AI can compose to reach new goals, and composing vetted parts is a very different risk than open-ended invention. If novelty is throttled at the plan level, the system can keep broad capabilities like internet access while doing only what was reviewed. Organizations already work this way: A hospital or bank approves standard operating procedures rather than vetting every decision. The AI equivalent is a reviewed plan, executed deterministically, with any deviation requiring new approval.​

The debate over AI safety and how quickly models should advance will continue, but enterprises can already build systems that keep increasingly capable AI within defined limits. Human control does not require understanding every decision a model makes. It requires ensuring that AI cannot decide the extent of its own authority.​

If you want to know what it looks like when a trillion-dollar tech bubble violently collides with physical reality, just look at yesterday. $2.5 trillion in tech valuations were wiped off the board as Wall Street panicked about AI’s leverage — punishing tech giants for incinerating cash on infrastructure that isn’t generating immediate profit.

Simultaneously, as we saw on Wednesday, the American voter rejected data center expansions in 40 out of 41 local ballot measures. The hardware hoarders are losing their grip, and the panic is palpable. The era of scrutiny is here, and I want to show you two possible timelines of where this could go.

But first, we have to go back over a couple things.

When faced with this stock crash, AMD CEO Lisa Su said, “We are a data center first company.” While I’d love to throw my hands up and get angry at this, I have to turn the BS detector on myself and address a brutal truth: she’s right. This market crash is a sentiment correction, not an overnight fab cancellation.

The big three memory foundries — SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron — operate on long-term agreements. 2026-2027 is already locked in at sky-high prices, and on top of that, enterprise AI accelerators consume roughly 3x the silicon wafers of standard consumer DDR5 memory.

As long as those massive AI server chips are shipping, conventional RAM capacity remains deeply suppressed.

So, if Wall Street is slashing valuations and data center permits are being blocked, why aren’t memory foundries pivoting back to consumer PC hardware right now?

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Hyperscalers are also starving for memory, and receive around 60-70% of what they ask for. If Microsoft and Meta get spooked by the market and pull back their massive order growth by 10% or even 15%, it wouldn’t trigger a supply chain pivot. It just means the foundries are a little less overwhelmed. Demand still vastly exceeds total factory capacity.

If foundries are still frantically trying to fulfill enterprise contracts, they have zero financial incentive to redirect back to consumer memory.

For them to actually panic and pivot, hyperscaler orders have to crater. A simple market correction like this won’t do it. But a sweeping wave of municipal zoning bans? That changes the math entirely.

Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence.November 4, 2026

If tech giants are legally barred from breaking ground on new server farms, they are forced to cancel their existing silicon orders because they physically have nowhere to plug the chips in.

We are not getting a massive surplus of GPUs and memory kits tomorrow morning. But the midterms and the stock market correction did put a concrete ceiling on the shortage. So let me take a stab at how I think this is going to unfold.

The stock rout has cracked the leveraged AI market for now, but contract prices remain firm. There is zero immediate relief, so don’t expect some banger Black Friday deals on RTX 5090s.

Memory shortages will hit their tightest consumer squeeze through early 2027. PC makers will fiercely defend a ceiling of 16GB-24GB on premium laptops and handhelds. If you’re hoping for 32GB in sub-$1,500 machines, shelve that hope through most of next year.

As hyperscalers face sustained stock and regulatory pressure from the midterm fallout, corporate boards will force company CFOs to look at their data center infrastructure plans again.

Instead of writing blank checks for server racks, the pace of subsequent purchase orders will slow. And for you reading this, I envision that PC hardware prices will finally stop climbing and plateau.

PC builders (Apple, Dell, Asus, Lenovo, etc) will gain massive leverage during mid-year procurement negotiations — putting an end to double-digit quarter-on-quarter price hikes.

A typical memory wafer run takes 3-4 months. Once the AI server orders officially ease in Q2, foundries will finally redirect their wafers back to consumer products. This is when the true price relief begins.

Standard desktop DDR5 kits will experience price drops, and holiday 2027 laptops will finally start normalizing 32GB unified configurations without severe margin penalties.

We aren’t completely out of the woods, and we still have to survive a brutal winter. But in my mind, those 2028 doom-and-gloom shortage predictions are officially dead.

The hyperscalers just hit a political and financial ceiling, which may lead to a peak in memory pricing this spring rather than running unchecked into next year.

Hold off on your PC upgrades — the local AI renaissance could be scheduled for the second half of 2027.

#3224. Not Nvidia. Not Palantir. The Midterms Just Made This Magnificent Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock the Safer Bet.

The Democratic Party won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections.

The 2026 midterm elections ended in a major political shake-up, with Democrats winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. While the results do not necessarily change the long-term outlook for artificial intelligence (AI), they could introduce new risks for some of the market's most popular AI stocks.

Companies such as Nvidia (NVDA -9.26%) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR -9.73%) have benefited enormously from the AI revolution so far. However, potential changes to federal spending priorities and greater scrutiny of AI infrastructure could complicate their growth trajectories going forward.

For investors looking to capitalize on the AI theme without taking on quite as much uncertainty, I think Microsoft (MSFT -3.58%) offers an interesting alternative.

Nvidia has become the backbone of the AI infrastructure boom. The company's graphics processing units (GPUs) power many of the data centers being built by Amazon (AMZN -2.19%), Microsoft, Alphabet (GOOGL -2.20%) (GOOG -1.93%), and Meta Platforms (META -3.96%).

However, data centers have become a political issue, particularly regarding electricity consumption, utility costs, and the strain on local infrastructure. Should the incoming Democratic Congress pursue tougher oversight or legislation affecting data center build-outs, hyperscalers could face higher development costs or longer approval timelines. In turn, this could cause big tech to reevaluate the pace of their infrastructure investments, potentially impacting demand for Nvidia's chips.

Palantir faces a different type of uncertainty. During the third quarter, the company generated $1.15 billion in government revenue, representing about half of its total sales. Although the company's commercial business is expanding rapidly, government contracting remains a key tailwind. If lawmakers pursue different defense spending priorities, Palantir could face a more challenging environment for securing new business from the public sector.

Microsoft is not completely immune to these risks. The company operates one of the top three largest cloud computing businesses in the world and is also investing heavily in AI infrastructure. However, what separates Microsoft from Nvidia and Palantir is the diversity of its revenue streams and business model.

Through Azure, Microsoft benefits directly from accelerating demand for AI compute. Meanwhile, products such as Microsoft 365, Windows, Dynamics, and cybersecurity software help generate additional recurring revenue. This means Microsoft can monetize AI through software subscriptions and enterprise productivity tools, even if the pace of data center construction eventually moderates. There is also an interesting regulatory distinction between Microsoft and its hyperscaler peers.

Amazon has faced an antitrust lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) since 2023, with regulators alleging that its online marketplace practices unfairly restrict competing e-commerce platforms and harm third-party sellers. Google has faced its share of legal setbacks, including a recent federal court ruling that it illegally monopolized certain digital advertising markets.

Meanwhile, Meta's regulatory challenges date back to a 2020 FTC lawsuit alleging that its acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp were designed to eliminate emerging competitors in the social media landscape. Although Meta won in court last November, the FTC appealed that decision in January -- keeping the dispute alive.

Microsoft has certainly faced regulatory scrutiny as well, including an investigation by the European Commission into bundling Teams with Microsoft 365. Still, I think its broad enterprise software ecosystem makes it an attractive way to invest in AI without relying as heavily on digital advertising or consumer platforms. While Microsoft is not politically untouchable, its combination of cloud infrastructure, established software properties, and recurring enterprise subscriptions offers multiple avenues for growth.

Microsoft's latest earnings results illustrate why its business model is so attractive. During its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (ended Sept. 30), revenue increased 19% year over year to $92.3 billion. Azure revenue soared 48%, while Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion.

Even more impressive, Microsoft's commercial remaining performance obligations (RPO) increased 73% to $677 billion. This figure represents contracted business that has yet to be recognized as revenue, providing meaningful visibility into future sales.

The company's cash flow is another important consideration. Microsoft generated $58 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, increasing 29% year over year. However, capital expenditures (capex) totaled $45.2 billion, reflecting the enormous costs of building AI infrastructure. This means Microsoft generated roughly $18.6 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, illustrating how data center investments are consuming a meaningful portion of its cash generation.

This creates an interesting potential upside scenario: If Microsoft moderates its infrastructure spending while continuing to monetize its existing cloud capacity and software ecosystem, free cash flow could improve substantially.

From a valuation perspective, Microsoft trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 27 following the election. While this is hardly a bargain in absolute terms, I think it's a reasonable premium for a company delivering double-digit revenue growth, expanding AI-driven cloud adoption, and generating recurring cash flow.

With a changing political landscape creating more uncertainty around infrastructure spending and federal contracts, Microsoft strikes me as a more balanced AI investment right now. For investors with a long-term time horizon, Microsoft may be one of the safer AI stocks to own following the midterms.
