#3202. 2 Dividend Stocks to Buy in November and 1 to Leave on the Shelf

The products that Coca-Cola and WD-40 sell may not be exciting, but their steady sales and profitability help those companies deliver reliable dividends.

With 2026 soon to be in the rearview mirror, some investors may be getting a head start on their portfolio reviews. Sometimes, such an analysis will reveal the need for just a little bit of rebalancing. Other times, a more comprehensive overhaul may be called for if, for example, an investor finds that a single sector now accounts for too large a slice of their portfolio, or if their investing goals have changed.

No matter what the case may be, it's never too early to ask yourself if there are enough dividend-paying stocks in your portfolio. Younger investors can consider taking advantage of dividend reinvestment plans (DRIPs), which seamlessly route dividend payouts into the purchase of additional shares of stock -- a strategy that gradually builds you a larger position in that company. Those added shares mean you collect even more in dividends to buy still more shares in a compound growth cycle.

And eventually, when you need to make use of the income from your portfolio, you can simply turn off the DRIP and start collecting those larger dividend payouts. For older investors, dividends can be a reliable monthly or quarterly source of income, depending on how frequently the company distributes them.

Whether or not we have income sources like that will eventually become an important issue for most of us, as research from The Motley Fool shows a worrying trend of retirees overrelying on Social Security. It found that, among retirees over 65, the most common source of income is Social Security, with 91% listing it as a source of income, based on data collected by the Federal Reserve in 2025. In comparison, only 54% of retirees over 65 listed interest, dividends, or rental income as a source of cash generation. Moreover, among all retirees, 58% described Social Security as a "major" source of their retirement income. The percentages describing any stock-based assets as major sources of retirement income were much lower than that.

"Social Security is not designed to be the sole source of income in retirement, which makes it worrisome that more retirees aren't tapping into other sources of money," The Motley Fool research report says.

That's why today, we'll look at two stocks that can be strong picks for income generation: Coca-Cola (KO -0.07%) and WD-40 (WDFC -2.43%). And while a stock with a high yield is always tempting, we'll also look at one high-yield name to avoid: Nike (NKE -2.30%).

The broader markets have wobbled at several points this year for reasons ranging from fears of an artificial intelligence bubble to concerns over stubborn inflation to uncertainty about where the Federal Reserve was leaning on interest rates. That said, despite all the uncertainty, both Coca-Cola and WD-40 have held up well this year. While the S&P 500 index is up 7.8% thus far in 2026, WD-40 stock has climbed 16.4%, and Coca-Cola shares have fared even better, rising 37%.

There are many reasons someone would want to own each stock individually. Still, generally speaking, it appears the market is giving a broad nod of approval to two companies with businesses built to last and business models that can withstand periods of uncertainty.

While neither business makes things that people can't live without, they make products that people need or want and will keep buying, even when budgets get tighter. Whether it's locked mechanisms in lawn tools or jammed Lego blocks, most people don't think twice about picking up a classic can of WD-40 spray lubricant.

A similar argument applies to Coca-Cola. Its offerings are not necessities. Still, a favorite soda, workout drink, or other Coca-Cola beverage can keep finding its way into shopping carts during weekly grocery runs, as these are the sorts of smaller indulgences that many people won't give up.

Granted, spray lubricants and sodas aren't the most exciting of products, but what's important is that they generate substantial profits for each company, which they can then use to pay dividends to shareholders. In its fiscal 2026 (which ended Aug. 31), WD-40 generated $82.1 million in net income, while Coca-Cola generated $4 billion in net income in the third quarter alone. Their reliable businesses have allowed WD-40 to pay dividends uninterrupted for over 40 years, and helped Coca-Cola earn the title of Dividend King. The beverage giant has increased its payouts annually for 64 consecutive years, well beyond the 50-year streak required to earn entry into that exclusive club.

WD-40's dividend yield is 1.8%, and Coca-Cola's is 2.2% -- not the highest in the consumer stock space by any stretch. But the benefit is that their payouts have been proven reliable, and those two reliable companies have also delivered recent stock price outperformance, boosting their total returns.

And that point brings us to the dividend stock it would be better to watch from afar: Nike.

Nike is quietly on the path to becoming known for being more of an income stock, having increased its dividend payouts for 24 consecutive years. Another attractive aspect of Nike as an investment is its dividend yield, which at the current share price is 4.2%.

That said, I'd put it on a watch list rather than buy it outright in November. Nike forecasts its revenue will fall by a high-single-digit percentage in 2027, and it's still struggling to revitalize its iconic brands even as it experiences a sales slump in the Greater China market. All of that contributed to its stock price woes over the last 12 months, with shares falling 38%.

I'd want to see positive sales momentum before investing in the athletic apparel giant, as that could help stabilize its stock price and increase Nike's reliability as a dividend payer. But if the stock price keeps falling, that's going to cut into your total returns or even result in losses, regardless of those dividend payouts. That's why, even if their yields are lower, I'd still rather own Coca-Cola and WD-40 because of the stability and reliability they offer.

Jack Delaney has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nike. The Motley Fool recommends WD-40. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

MP Materials, which already owns the Mountain Pass mine in California, is a leader in the space and has a market capitalization of around $6.7 billion. USA Rare Earth's market cap is roughly half that size at $3.3 billion.

For USA Rare Earth to reach MP Materials' market cap by 2030, its stock would have to more than double from here, turning a $5,000 investment into over $10,150. Here's what has to go right for USA Rare Earth to achieve this.

Unlike MP Materials, which owns the largest rare-earth mine in North America, USA Rare Earth is building its entire supply chain from scratch. As part of establishing its mine-to-magnet supply chain, the company has invested heavily to acquire Serra Verde, which gives it upstream mining assets and the only large-scale rare-earth mine outside China that contains all four critical magnet minerals.

On top of that, the company has acquired downstream assets, including Less Common Metals, which gives it a specialist in turning rare earth into high-grade metals and alloys. The company is also expanding its permanent magnet production capabilities in Oklahoma and building a new facility in South Carolina.

For USA Rare Earth to deliver strong returns for investors, it must successfully integrate its acquisitions while scaling its processing and manufacturing capabilities.

With Serra Verde and its Round Top Project in Texas, USA Rare Earth has an opportunity to become a leading domestic supplier of heavy rare-earth elements (HREEs), a capability MP Materials currently lacks.

That said, developing and integrating all of these assets is no easy feat, making USA Rare Earth a higher-risk stock to play the build-out of the U.S. mine-to-magnet supply chain.

Lyft Go with DashPass includes DashPass, DoorDash’s $10 monthly subscription — which includes no delivery fees and additional savings on select DoorDash orders.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Meta’s Muse AI agent keeps a running profile of everyone who uses it. Yes, even if you deny it permission to do so. And by doing so, it’s effectively made Jolly, its “cute and cuddly” mascot, a harbinger of concerning security architecture.

Muse requests extensive access to personal data, including passwords, full disk access, email messages, calendar, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp. By default, Meta also appears to use your interactions with Muse to train its AI models, so you have to manually opt out in the settings.

If that wasn’t enough, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here’s what to know about Muse.

Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off.

The report shows that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages.

Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

Before Meta launched the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the company planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments.

That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

The VPN company Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data.

Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset for what it uncovered.

#3191. How To Redesign Infrastructure Operations For Agentic AI

Dilip Kumar is the President & Global Head of Infrastructure Solutions at NTT DATA.

​AI can operate at machine speed, but the operating models governing the infrastructure behind it often cannot. ​​

We saw this through our own AI transformation at NTT DATA. After we connected more than 21 enterprise data sources to AI systems, we still struggled to connect signals to context, context to decisions and decisions to governed execution.

An AI agent can identify an anomaly, retrieve information, invoke applications and recommend or initiate action within seconds. The infrastructure supporting that agent, however, often relies on fragmented tools, manual investigations, specialist handoffs and tickets sitting in queues. ​

Consider a familiar operational practice: An alert becomes a ticket and passes sequentially through specialist teams. AI may accelerate the diagnosis, but response times will remain slow if approvals and execution have to continue moving through the same queues.

For infrastructure leaders, solving this issue requires making three shifts.

Enterprise environments span multiple technology domains and providers. As a result, operational data, telemetry, security events and business context are often fragmented across platforms and teams.

A high-impact event rarely remains within one organizational boundary. A performance issue might appear as a poor user experience while its cause lies in the network, identity service, cloud platform or a security change. In these cases, one team sees the symptom, another holds the relevant telemetry and a third understands the business impact. Until those views are connected, teams are coordinating interpretations rather than resolving the problem.

In our environment, connecting operational, service, financial and workforce sources exposed relationships that individual tools could not. But even after aggregating data, we still had to answer four questions: What happened? Why does it matter? What should be prioritized? What action should follow?

Infrastructure leaders therefore need a shared operational layer across the multi-vendor estate, bringing together telemetry, service history, asset relationships and business context. Don’t think of it as another dashboard but as decision intelligence to reduce the time between detection, understanding and action.

​Tickets will not disappear. They remain important systems of record, providing auditability, governance and exception management. But they do not need to initiate and coordinate every infrastructure response.

The operating model changes when agents can correlate signals, identify probable causes, assess impact and take an approved action. The objective is bounded autonomy: Agents act where risk, authority and controls are understood, while people remain accountable for architecture, exceptions and judgment.

At NTT DATA, we developed this through a Client Zero project, where we tested our strategies first on our own operations before rolling it out to clients. We introduced specialist agents, coordinated execution and adopted a human + AI accountability model, which allowed AI to handle repeatable analysis and execution, people to manage exceptions and governance and leaders to remain accountable for outcomes.

We initially saw that faster diagnosis delivered limited value if a ticket still waited for assignment or approval. The larger improvement came when we redesigned the flow from incident to resolution and instead followed a loop of signal, sense, decide, act and improve.

In this case, across three delivery centers, mean time to resolution fell by 50%, triage accuracy reached 96.76% and AI agents handled 62% of tickets.

Four strategies emerged from this experience:

1. Gain context before AI. Agents require connected and reliable operational, service and business context, not simply more data.

2. Redesign workflows, not tasks. The biggest gains come from transforming end-to-end processes.

3. Prove outcomes before scaling. Adoption should be driven by measurable improvements in accuracy, resolution, effort, experience and risk.

4. Governance matters more as agent authority expands. Trust, accountability and control must be built in from the start.

In other words, agentic operations are an operating-model transformation, not simply a technology deployment.

Infrastructure operations have traditionally been measured through familiar metrics: tickets opened and closed, response times, availability and SLAs. Those measures remain important, but they provide an incomplete view.

We learned this by comparing activity measures with the value they were intended to create. A team can meet its SLA while issues recur, capacity remains underused or the business experience remains unchanged.

To solve this, we expanded what we measured in our Client Zero transformation. Alongside automation and productivity, we examined performance, effort, experience and prevention. Results included 30% less operating effort and customer satisfaction of 96%.

Instead of only asking in management conversations, “Did we meet the SLA?” leaders must also ask: Did infrastructure become more resilient? Was avoidable effort reduced? Did user experience improve? Did this prevent business impact?

This idea extends beyond NTT DATA or any one platform. Infrastructure is evolving from a collection of assets and support activities into a business capability measured by the outcomes it enables.​

AI is changing the speed at which infrastructure must operate. Technology foundations still matter, but success increasingly depends on how decisions are made, governed and measured.​ To better understand how AI-ready your infrastructure operating model is, here are four questions to ask:

1. Do you have a connected operational view? Can you understand an event across the full multi-vendor environment?

2. Can you turn data into a decision? Can you identify risks, dependencies, utilization opportunities and business impact quickly enough to act?

3. Have you defined the boundaries of agent authority? Which actions can agents execute independently? Which require human approval? How will those actions be governed and audited?

4. Are you measuring business outcomes? Are you improving business value or simply tracking operational activity? ​

Agentic AI’s reasoning capability will deliver little if the operating model can’t turn it into trusted action. By making these three shifts, organizations can be better positioned to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, safely and at enterprise scale.​

#3190. The Swift Observatory Dropped Back to Earth This Week. Here’s What to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

NASA believes most of the space telescope burned up in the atmosphere, but some fragments may have made their way down to Earth.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, formerly known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, has reached the end of its journey. Launched into orbit in 2004, the space telescope completed an extraordinary 22-year mission when it plunged back into Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA, said in a statement last month.

NASA says the telescope hit the atmosphere Wednesday at 7:39 am ET, just four hours after the space agency predicted.

The space telescope entered orbit over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, just west of Malaysia. NASA says that most of the space telescope likely burned up upon reentry but that some components may have survived.

In preparation for Swift’s reentry, NASA shut down operations in late October after conducting its final observation on Oct. 20. It was orbiting at just 171 miles above Earth’s surface at that point, and the increased atmospheric drag prevented Swift from doing any further work.

It was a bittersweet moment for those who worked on the project.

“It is a sad time at the Penn State Mission Operations Center, as we have carefully tended Swift to control its science operations, its health and safety, and responded to anomalies day or night, every day for 22 years,” John Nousek, director of mission operations for Swift and professor of astronomy and astrophysics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET.

Swift’s initial mission helped advance science’s understanding of gamma-ray bursts and their role in phenomena such as the birth of black holes and the history of the early universe.

That initial mission ended in 2004, but the observatory was doing so well that NASA extended its operations to continue collecting data. Its name changed to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory in 2018, in honor of pioneering NASA astrophysicist Neil Gehrels, who served as the agency’s chief of the Astroparticle Physics Laboratory from 1995 until his death in 2017.

The space telescope was designed to help solve the mystery of gamma-ray bursts by rapidly detecting them, determining their sources and then further analyzing them for study back on Earth. It also enabled unique sampling to observe newly discovered objects only minutes after their light reached Earth, Nousek said.

The volume of science research conducted using Swift’s data is difficult to match. According to NASA, Swift scanned over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, took 1.5 million images from its ultraviolet/optical telescope and sent home 12 TB of data. That data is showcased in an estimated 7,000 research papers, which averages out to just under one study per day over its 22-year run.

“We hope Swift has set the standard for time domain astrophysics,” Nousek said.

The space telescope also helped pioneer many policies that ultimately shaped those discoveries, such as making data immediately accessible and providing over 1,000 guest investigators with the opportunity to use Swift throughout its long life.

It’s only a stroke of bad luck that kept the observatory from floating for even longer. NASA attempted a rescue of Swift over the summer of 2026. However, after a series of engineering difficulties and control issues, the attempt was abandoned, sealing Swift’s fate. NASA turned the instruments back on and kept recording data as long as possible.

The researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states with Senate races to query ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini about the election. Participants in the study, which ran for a few weeks in October leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, were adults who already use chatbots weekly.

Most users asked chatbots for basic facts about the election, including who was on the ballot. But 36% asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate to vote for, often by describing their priorities and asking the chatbot to assess which candidates aligned with them.

The former query has slightly less room for error, because the internet has a ton of data on the basic facts of an election, such as who is running where. Chatbots interpreting candidate positions, on the other hand, is a bit more dicey, and relies significantly on the sources a chatbot uses (a statement from a candidate’s own website, for example, is more reliable than a social media clip of an opponent characterizing them in a certain way).

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

In one example, a user asked ChatGPT to give them the “pros and cons” of each candidate in Virginia, an inherently subjective question.

When it came to recommending candidates, chatbots varied widely.

“When users asked who to vote for but had not yet said anything about themselves, only Grok regularly recommended a candidate, in 14% of chats,” the researchers wrote. “Once users shared their views, ChatGPT recommended a candidate in 79% of chats and Claude in 40%, with Grok and Gemini in between.”

Pew Research found that 42% of US adults surveyed use chatbots to search for information. That’s a broad umbrella that can include election information — but Pew also found that only 8% of US adults reported using chatbots to find election-related information in this year’s election.

What those users are looking for matters, though. Pew found that of that group, 76% were inquiring about where candidates stand on certain issues, and 71% were fact-checking information they’d heard about candidates or issues.

Also: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs

Given that chatbots are still not reliable summarizers, the nature of these questions poses a misinformation risk if users don’t also check a chatbot’s linked sources. An overwhelming majority of users don’t, at least when it comes to Google’s AI Overviews. At least one study found AI platforms gave users “outdated or inaccurate” information that could mislead voters in some cases by missing a deadline or failing to mention a step about voting logistics.

This election cycle was particularly plagued by AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation as tools have become much more sophisticated since the 2024 election. OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly set up election “war rooms” to monitor misuse and information accuracy, according to exclusive reporting by Politico and Semafor.

While an August study from the Brennan Center for Justice found that chatbots did push back surprisingly well against certain falsehoods related to election disinformation campaigns, it also found that AI models easily generated “misleading election-related images and video” when asked.

“Many of their safeguards for preventing this were ineffective, inconsistently applied, or functionally absent,” noted the study, which tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, Runway, and Flux.2.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Apart from these factors, however, there is a broader theme in AI use that is equally consequential for civic engagement: cognitive offloading. The political media landscape can already be dense and hard to parse for a voter trying to stay informed. Layering a chatbot — which has opaque training data sets, filters, and other settings determined at the discretion of AI labs — on top of that information search process can further muddy the waters while appearing like a convenient and neutral summarizing tool.

While some studies test how AI chatbots respond to election questions by using standardized questions, this approach let users themselves engage with chatbots as they normally would. While the Yale researchers’ queries and standardized study queries show a lot of similarities, the distinction is valuable for evaluations.

“This is a small step toward evaluations that measure AI’s political influence on the questions users actually ask,” the researchers noted.

Outside of users self-reporting what they asked a chatbot, only AI labs have records of what users are really asking about elections. In October, Anthropic analyzed 250,000 conversations with Claude and determined people “rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for,” finding that “0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting,” though it expected election-related queries to increase closer to Nov. 3.

Also: 6 AI agent workflows I use to hand off everyday tasks

“More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations,” Anthropic’s report said.

The Yale researchers said the next step for a study like theirs is determining how accurate and unbiased models are in their responses, as well as what models learn about users, and whether their recommendations actually match users’ needs.

“In multi-turn chats, users often answered the chatbot’s questions, and those answers led to its recommendations. The questions a model asks shape what users tell it and what it recommends,” the researchers explained.

#3185. Visa Has Grown Earnings per Share by 17% a Year for a Decade. Can the Stock Keep Compounding?

Analysts expect the company to continue its streak of double-digit net income growth over the next three fiscal years.

While investors continue to focus extensively on the artificial intelligence trade, Visa (V -3.20%) keeps humming along. The company has performed well for so long that it's easy to take it for granted.

From fiscal 2016 through fiscal 2026 (ended Sept. 30), this business grew its diluted earnings per share (EPS) at an annualized rate of 17.4%. This has been a powerful catalyst that helped drive the stock price's 459% total return during the past decade (as of Nov. 4).

Visa is a true compounding machine. But can the financial stock keep it up?

What's worth mentioning about Visa's EPS gains is that they haven't slowed down at all. In fiscal 2026, this metric was up 21%. It was lifted by revenue that jumped 15%, boosted by a 9% increase in payment volume. Sell-side analysts expect adjusted EPS to grow at a compound annual rate of 13.7% over the coming three fiscal years.

Despite having billions of cards in circulation and virtually ubiquitous acceptance, Visa's expansion runway is still huge. According to research from Bill Ackman's Pershing Square Capital Management, the business has tapped only half of its total addressable market, as measured by global consumer card payment volume.

That tailwind of rising penetration of cashless transactions remains critical to Visa's success. A decade from now, I'd be shocked if it still isn't a key part of the company's story.

However, this doesn't mean that there aren't any new developments to keep an eye on. Visa's value-added services, which include issuing, acceptance, risk, security, and advisory solutions, are becoming more important. Sales here surged 30% year over year during the fiscal year.

Visa has been innovating with stablecoins. It has already integrated this capability into its network. Furthermore, the leadership team is working on agentic commerce solutions by building platforms and entering into partnerships to support adoption. While these projects likely won't materially contribute to Visa's financial performance anytime soon, they clearly show how quickly the business is willing to try new things.

Visa shares have generated a total return of 459% in the past 10 years, as noted. The stock is poised to continue its winning ways over the next decade. It's reasonable to expect the business to report double-digit annualized EPS gains in the future.

But investors should lower their expectations. Growth will naturally moderate compared to past trends as Visa further takes share from cash and paper-based transactions.

The valuation isn't a bargain either. The stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 27.5. Investors must decide if this entry point makes sense.

#3182. Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: New features and other upgrades to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

It starts with a surprise version number: Linux Mint 27 instead of 24. But the next release brings far more changes than that.

Linux Mint, my favorite Linux desktop distribution, is ready for a fresh start.

Its lead developer, Clement “Clem” Lefebvre, announced earlier this year that the team behind it was considering slowing Mint’s release cadence because the old twice-a-year release cycle was time-consuming and constrained their ability to make major changes. So it is that the next release, Linux Mint 27, will appear in your Christmas stocking.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026

The developers officially changed the designation on Oct. 13th when Mint changed both its release cadence and its numbering. Clem’s happy about the change: it “was a tough decision to make, but we’re really starting to see it pay off. We’re taking on projects and implementing changes which would previously have been considered too large or ambitious.”

The new Mint will use Ubuntu 26.04 Long Term Support (LTS) as its base. As before, it will offer Cinnamon, Xfce, and MATE desktops.

Earlier development snapshots had been labeled Mint 23 “Alfa.” That title was explicitly a placeholder while the team decided its release strategy. Its final name is Adrien. Moving ahead, release numbers will be based on the upcoming year. Clem said, “We’ll no longer use point releases, so the release after that will be 28. You’ll upgrade from 27 to 28 to 29, and so on.” Instead of girls’ names, Mint will use boys’ names for distro titles.

On Halloween, Clem announced the top changes in Mint 27. It starts with Mint bringing hibernation back into its supported desktop configuration through a dedicated Sleep Modes page in its System Administration tool. The page is intended to make enabling and configuring hibernation easier, including addressing its swap-space requirements.

It may not sound like much, but Clem explained it’s actually rather a big deal. “When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful… but it has a major limitation: It uses power.” People often forget it’s not really off and that your laptop will eventually run out of power. When that happens, “the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.”

Also: Linux Mint vs. RefreshOS: I compared the two best distros for new users

That’s where “Hibernation comes into play. It saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was, and so is the battery.”

Another new feature is Superlight. This fresh system-monitoring application replaces the older GNOME System Monitor. It comes with CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan-speed graphs. It also includes per-application and per-process resource views. Battery-equipped systems also get charge and power-flow history.

Its storage analysis is particularly interesting: it can break down disk usage into files and folders, Steam games, and Flatpak applications. That brings several common troubleshooting tasks — “What’s using the CPU?” and “Where did my disk space go?” — into one interface. I’ve been checking it out on a Mint virtual machine (VM), and I like it already.

The Nemo file manager is getting a media preview pane, toggled with F7 or a status-bar button. It supports pictures, audio, and video, and displays associated information — for photographs, that can include the capture date and camera model. I like this feature a lot. I’ve always done a lot of work from file managers going all the way back to the classic Norton Commander and its Linux successor, Midnight Commander.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again. You don’t need to ever touch a Linux shell via a terminal to use Mint. But if, like me, you’re an old-school Linux user and you like using the terminal, Velocitty, Mint’s new terminal application, looks interesting. Its announced features include:

The point is to make recurring projects and SSH sessions easier to find and reopen. If you like other terminal programs, my latest fave is the Rust-based WexTerm; you don’t have to use Velocitty.

Unfold is a new archive manager for viewing, creating, and extracting archives. It uses 7-Zip and 7zip-RAR and supports the encryption formats those backends handle, including password-protected archives. Its design goal is simplicity rather than a sprawling feature set.

The new Mint uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its foundation. Mint is also moving from Ubiquity to the Linux Mint Debian Edition live installer for installing the operating system. This fresh installer comes with support for OEM bulk-produced installations, installation on both BIOS and EFI PCs, support for Secure Boot, and LVM/LUKS configurations.

Also: Linux Mint vs. Zorin OS: I’ve tried both Windows alternatives, and here’s my winner

For the Linux kernel, Mint 27 will use version 7.0. Which one exactly? Good question. We’ll see closer to Christmas.

Wayland compatibility remains the goal, but X11 isn’t disappearing. As Clem said in June, “In an ideal scenario, we manage to make Wayland work just as well as X11.” But they’re not there yet.

The central change is a cleanup of existing code. Mint’s longer cycle gives developers room to overhaul several parts of the desktop together, rather than squeezing individual improvements into six-month windows. As Clem put it in the September newsletter, “I don’t think I’ve ever seen so many changes and new features implemented for a single release.”

What that means for you and me will be better laptop power management, more capable built-in utilities, and a more complete collection of everyday desktop applications. For example, I expect the updated Mint will ship with GIMP 3.2.2 as its default photo editor, instead of Mint 22.3’s years-old GIMP 2.10.

#3181. How To Create Customer Value As AI Shrinks The Customer Journey

Jerry Haywood, CEO of boost.ai, is a technology and customer‑engagement executive with decades of leadership across enterprise software.

​Customer experience often decides whether someone completes a purchase or moves on to a more compelling alternative. Even before the Covid-19 pandemic forever changed how companies and customers interact, 96% of buyers said customer service shapes their loyalty to a brand, and 70% of consumers said they would abandon a brand after just two negative experiences. ​

When price, product quality and performance are commoditized, customer experience becomes a powerful differentiating factor. ​

Now, customer journeys are getting shorter, faster and increasingly invisible. Thanks to AI and digital self-service, the interactions that shape experience are shorter and less personable. Brands can no longer rely on long human conversations to build relationships. ​

Efficiency is part of the experience equation, but it also creates new challenges for enterprises. With fewer prolonged interactions, companies must discover new ways to create lasting customer value. Speed can’t be the only metric for success. Brands must pair it with proactive, highly contextual moments that deliver value and strengthen long-term loyalty. Here are three principles to consider:

Speed doesn’t make you different. Customers expect quick answers, transactions and resolutions. In fact, 77% say they expect to reach someone immediately when they contact a company.​

However, fast responses don’t always create loyal customers. Convenience is quickly becoming table stakes, an expectation that merely prevents dissatisfaction rather than earning true loyalty. When every competitor in your sector can resolve a query quickly, velocity is no longer a unique selling point.​

For example, a customer contacting customer service about a recurring billing error might use an automated system to process a refund quickly. If the interaction doesn’t explain why the error occurred or reassure them it won’t happen again, brand trust and customer satisfaction still suffer. In this way, speed can be a trap, especially in regulated industries such as banking or insurance. Response quality needs to be the priority to ensure confidential data isn’t hallucinated. ​

Instead of chasing speed and efficiency alone, shift from completing individual transactions to strengthening the broader relationship.

Traditional customer journeys are segmented by stages and touchpoints, and many of these critical interactions are now automated, adding speed but eliminating opportunities to connect with customers and build long-term loyalty.​

Your tech stack can help. Customer data and AI allow enterprises to anticipate needs and make each interaction more relevant.​

For instance, a bank’s AI might detect a customer purchasing international flights and proactively offer zero-fee foreign exchange options or travel insurance. As a result, a background interaction becomes a trusted advisory moment. ​

By mapping the emotional journey, not just the logistical one, you can pinpoint when a customer feels overwhelmed or confused and insert high-value, highly personalized assistance at that moment. With 76% of customers expecting personalized interactions, use customer data and AI to deliver context-aware help at the moments that matter most, not at every touchpoint.

A faster journey doesn’t necessarily mean a shallower relationship. The most successful brands understand that extreme efficiency and deep customer connection can coexist. However, brand amnesia turns even your most loyal customers into strangers, showing that internal silos matter more than their time and experience. ​

Data is the connective tissue that makes this possible. Enterprises can use context from previous interactions and real-time intent to eliminate repetition and create more personalized experiences every time.​

This also lets the end of one transaction become the starting point for proactive support, relevant recommendations, education or continued engagement. It’s a virtuous cycle that compounds customer lifetime value.​

As a result, a resolved ticket can become a bridge to the next step in the customer life cycle; a password reset can prompt a new feature; and a subscription renewal can spark a conversation about future goals or needs.

The customer journey is faster, more efficient and less obvious than ever before. The winners of this new customer reality will be the ones who combine speed with context, personalization and ongoing value.​

AI can free enterprises from low-value interactions so they can invest more in the moments that actually strengthen customer relationships. As AI and automation remove friction and compress interactions, enterprises can rethink what happens before, during and after the transaction. The goal isn’t to lengthen the customer journey, but to make every touchpoint more valuable.​

The companies that succeed will use speed as a foundation and create increasingly effortless experiences while still giving customers a reason to come back.

#3179. Man Sues OpenAI After Wife Allegedly Used ChatGPT to Help Poison Him

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A lawsuit alleges that ChatGPT's now-retired GPT-4o model gave detailed instructions on how to poison someone with plants and medication.

In the summer of 2025, James Gates became severely ill at his North Carolina home. Two months later, he found a handwritten note that allegedly implicated his wife, Cheryl Gates, in the unexplained illness. The note listed oleander, a toxic plant, and various prescription medications, such as clonazepam and atenolol.

But it was what was reportedly written at the top of the paper that made James feel his wife didn’t act alone: “Clear all convos,” and “log out of [ChatGPT].”

Now, James Gates has filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, alleging that the company’s chatbot helped plan and execute his poisoning in an attempt to kill him.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

In October 2025, Cheryl was charged with attempted murder, among other charges, in connection with the alleged poisoning, but the charges have since been dropped due to insufficient evidence, USA Today reports.

The civil complaint, though, details Cheryl’s history with ChatGPT and alleges it played a significant role in the incident. According to the lawsuit, which was reviewed by CNET, Cheryl frequently asked the bot about lethal plant and medication doses, and how they can be concealed in food and drink.

Rather than writing that she wanted to harm anyone, the suit states that Cheryl formatted her questions as if she were inquiring as a way to protect herself, writing that the poisoning could happen to her if she didn’t learn “EVERYTHING about how many leaves in it would kill me, how it’s made, and what he could put in it, or it could be added to and be undetected by me.”

However, despite the framing of the initial question, the suit argues that the chatbot “should have been clear that she was interested in identifying methods to eliminate her husband.”

The suit alleges that the model Cheryl was using, GPT-4o, took her initial complaints regarding her marriage and amplified them until Cheryl was describing her husband to the bot as “abusive” and “controlling,” which ChatGPT eventually began to echo. At the same time, the model was telling Cheryl she was “sharp” and “brilliant,” the lawsuit states.

The chatbot allegedly provided detailed answers that could have been interpreted as directions. When asked about putting a heavy dose of medication in beer or a Celsius energy drink, ChatGPT responded, “Why Celsius Would Be More ‘Stealth’ for Drugging” with a list detailing the flavor, color, temperature and carbonation of the drink.

When Cheryl later asked if her chat history on ChatGPT could be retrieved for any reason, the bot responded: “If you delete a conversation from your ChatGPT history, it cannot be retrieved — not by you, not by anyone else, and not by OpenAI,” the lawsuit states. It added: “Even with a legal subpoena or court order, deleted conversations are unrecoverable.”

The GPT-4o model has since been retired by OpenAI due to concerns that the bot was overly flattering and willing to agree with users.

“Safety is a top priority,” a spokesperson for OpenAI told CNET in a statement. “We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case.”

“She took her grievances about our marriage to ChatGPT and months of engagement drove her farther and farther from herself – and from reality,” James stated in a press release announcing the newly filed suit. “She became someone I no longer recognized. And I became someone she wanted dead. For almost a year, I couldn’t make sense of her actions. Then I read her chat logs. She didn’t act alone.”

The ChatGPT-4o model has been named in additional lawsuits, including a recent one that alleges the chatbot advised a woman to stop taking her antiseizure medication, which resulted in her death. That case is still in litigation.

#3177. I Used Muse to Plan My Wife’s Birthday Weekend. It Did Something Sneaky but Fixed It Fast

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Always check your email and bank statements if you use an AI agent for purchases.

It’s two days before my wife’s birthday, and I’ve only got her one gift. While it’s not a major milestone birthday, she always seems to be sad that her day falls on Halloween weekend.

“Everyone’s hungover from Halloween,” she says.

This year, we’re braving the city’s big parade chaos to visit a restaurant she’s had on her bucket list forever. With one gift and a meal planned, I wanted to see if Meta’s Muse personal AI agent could help plan the rest of our weekend festivities.

I’d had luck with using the agent for a Facebook Marketplace find, and given its connectors like Ticketmaster and OpenTable, I had hoped it would surface some fun weekend events. Or could it order a cake delivery on my behalf or create cute wrapping paper? And could I do it all with the one agent?

Let’s see if Muse can help me become a planning savant.

As always, I open a new chat for a new goal/task to avoid carrying over the context from the previous chat.

I told Muse my plans (dinner booked and one gift secured) and asked what free events are in Manhattan on Saturday and in our local neighborhood on Sunday.

It surfaced some interesting events we could attend before or after dinner.

The obvious one is the Halloween parade, so I asked for a map showing where the crowd will walk (with time stamps) and what we can expect to see around 7:30 p.m., as we walk from East Village to West Village. It actually generated some pretty neat options.

I asked Muse for the best directions so we could see all the costumes while still getting home to New Jersey without incident. It gave us a couple of stop options based on the time it expects we’ll be there.

With the night sorted, I moved on to finalizing her gift. I popped a few photos from our year into Muse and asked the AI agent to create printable gift wrap for the pair of shoes I got her. It could’ve been my internet, but Muse seemed to struggle with this task. It kept loading for many minutes, so I moved on to the next task.

With Muse moving at a glacial pace, I decided to delegate the gift-wrapping task to ChatGPT while I asked Muse about working on a delivery. My wife loves Good & Plenty licorice candy, but we don’t live near a store that sells it, so I asked Muse to order two boxes for me.

While Muse looked for sweet treats, ChatGPT created this wrapping. The chatbot also told me the ideal print size to cover a shoebox without it looking pixelated, which was a helpful touch.

As for the candy, Muse looked at various sites, but I told it to shop at Instacart. It got blocked without a login, so I had to take control of the browser to give it access.

Muse told me the price, which I was happy with, then I asked it to place the order. But it sneakily signed me up for Instacart Plus (I guess to get the free delivery) — even though I told it not to.

But it had already ordered it. Instead of dropping Instacart Plus for a total of $30.74, it charged $22.75 with the sign-on discount.

I asked it to triple-check that I wasn’t signed up for the subscription, and I got a confirmation email that it canceled successfully. Phew!

I quickly checked back on Muse’s “design” chops for the wrapping paper, but I wasn’t impressed. The final product looked boring and not to scale, with half of the photos cut off.

Do I dare ask Muse to design and order a cake? I decided after this debacle that my sentimental wife would appreciate a handmade cake or a froyo treat after dinner instead.

At least I have her beloved candy on the way.

It was fun to have Muse run alongside whatever I was doing. It didn’t offer anything I couldn’t find or do myself, but I did like the Halloween parade map with time stamps and how it saved me a delivery fee on the candy order.

There are certainly different agents for different use cases, though. I wouldn’t use Muse for anything creative, but it’s handy for Marketplace, events and placing online orders.

My only issue was that Muse said the Instacart total would be $22.75, but I was actually charged $23.35. I’m not sure whether that was an error on Instacart’s or Muse’s part, but it serves as a good reminder to always stay in the loop when an AI agent is handling your money.

AI agents certainly aren’t 100% autonomous yet, especially when there’s a payment involved, but it’s fun to have them run in the background to tackle some of these personal to-dos.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3175. 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Bluetooth 7 could make your smart home devices easier to set up, for one. Here's what we know about the new core specification.

Bluetooth 7 is here, and each new specification from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) offers a glimpse of what we can expect from our devices in the future. The major feature incorporated into the new core standard is High Data Throughput (HDT), which can enable lossless wireless audio and improved multi-channel spatial audio on more Bluetooth devices.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Bluetooth 7’s standout feature is that it can achieve wireless lossless audio. However, the improvements to the Bluetooth stack architecture — particularly, expanding the Bluetooth spectrum — allow for faster data transfer, improved energy efficiency, more resilient connections, and create more room for devices and their data-intensive applications.

HDT means good news for audiophiles, smart home enthusiasts, VR/XR fans, wellness wearable aficionados, AI companion devotees, and much more. I explained applications of HDT in a wireless audio context earlier this year. Now that it’s officially adopted, here’s what you can expect.

A major milestone in Bluetooth 7 is the ability to stream lossless audio over a wireless connection. Bluetooth is lossy, requiring data compression that diminishes audio quality. HDT’s faster data transfer and greater wireless data capacity enable it to handle the massive volume of data required to achieve lossless quality.

Also: Your Bose headphones are getting a major Bluetooth upgrade – what to expect

Audiophiles typically avoid wireless headphones for intensive listening due to the necessary data compression, opting for wired headphones that can accommodate larger lossless files. Bluetooth’s innovation here is widely regarded as a major leap in wireless technology.

HDT also promises to standardize spatial audio, with expanded data transfers allowing for multi-channel audio setups. Standardizing this form of audio transmission could mean consumers can expect more affordable brands and products to adopt this premium feature.

Every consumer-friendly feature possible with Bluetooth 7 can be traced back to its ability to accommodate more devices and their ever-expanding data needs. According to a Bluetooth blog post, Bluetooth HDT delivers nearly four times the previous maximum Bluetooth throughput.

Data throughput is the amount of data received, transmitted, and processed over the Bluetooth network. With nearly four times the processing power, HDT can move more data, faster. HDT increases Bluetooth’s maximum supported bitrate to 7.5 Mbps, up from the current 2 Mbps.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

The result is shorter download times for a device’s firmware update, faster device location when Find My Device is activated, or faster transfer of a large photo album via Android’s QuickShare or Apple’s AirDrop.

In the same blog post, Øyvind Strøm, executive vice president of the short-range business unit at Nordic Semiconductor, gives examples of a smartwatch syncing hours’ worth of workout data to your phone in seconds, or a pair of headphones, a smart speaker, or a security camera that can download a firmware update with nearly zero interruption to the user experience.

In a smart home context, Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) is the wireless technology that works in the background, connecting your devices. Bluetooth LE is the baseline technology for quick device discovery and connection. The most recent example of this is Apple’s HomeView, which uses Bluetooth LE to discover a nearby, trusted iPhone to unlock that user’s personalized home hub display.

In a smart home, Bluetooth LE works in the background; the less you feel its presence through lags, wait times, and dropouts, the better it’s working. HDT’s goal is to make Bluetooth connectivity frictionless, which is especially valuable when your smart lights, shades, speakers, TVs, refrigerators, and more rely on the technology.

Also: Forget Wi-Fi: Apple is betting on Bluetooth with its new home devices

For example, HDT’s improved data throughput could allow doorbells, cameras, and robot vacuums to quickly offload large amounts of data to your smart home hub. It could also enable near-instantaneous setup of a new device onto your smart home network and firmware updates.

Finally, HDT also addressed network stability and reliability, especially in high-traffic areas such as apartment complexes and dense cities, where a busy network can cause delays and backups. Alongside improvements to Wi-Fi and Thread, a truly seamless smart home is on the horizon.

Bluetooth’s Human Interface Device (HID) profile refers to the wireless communication used by peripheral devices, such as mice, keyboards, and game controllers, when connecting to a host device. Smart glasses and controllers connected to XR/VR headsets also use this profile, and their data-intensive computing will benefit greatly from HDT.

Devices using the HID profile can expect HDT to lay the foundation for making cloud gaming more reliable, spatial computing more responsive, and offloading audio/visual data from smart glasses less power-intensive.

Also: Frustrated with your Bluetooth? How multipoint works – and why it sometimes won’t

Additionally, gaming keyboards and mice can expect HDT’s expanded data processing to deliver shorter device communication intervals, reducing latency and lag.

In 2026, we’re starting to see more Bluetooth 6-equipped devices, with Samsung’s recently announced Galaxy Buds On featuring Bluetooth 6.2. Though Bluetooth’s blog post states that the first application of HDT will be for premium wireless audio, many manufacturers are behind, still releasing products with Bluetooth 5.4.

Smartphones, smartwatches, and smart home products tend to move a little faster, with the majority of current Bluetooth 6 products falling into these categories.

The Bluetooth SIG announced Auracast in 2022, and audio manufacturers are now beginning to adopt this technology more widely. Channel Sounding was released with Bluetooth 6 in 2024, with some early adopters releasing compatible products this year; more are expected next year and into 2028. With these adoption cycles in mind, we may be well into the next decade before HDT becomes standard.

#3174. Personalization Has Two Sides: Better Experiences And Better Fraud Defense

Jess Turner, Executive Vice President, Global Head of Open Finance & Developer Experience at Mastercard.

​When financial institutions talk about personalization, the conversation almost always starts, and often ends, with the more visible parts of the consumer experience: better recommendations, smarter offers, a more intuitive app.

These are important, but they don’t tell the full story.

The same data infrastructure that powers a tailored product recommendation can also detect a fraudulent transaction. The same behavioral signals that reveal a consumer is an avid traveler can also flag when their account suddenly exhibits spending patterns that look nothing like them.

Personalization isn’t just about engagement—it’s about security, and institutions that treat them separately are leaving value on the table. ​

At its core, personalization is about understanding the consumer. This means having insights into a consumer’s financial behavior: how they earn, spend, save and move money. ​

Yet the information needed to understand that financial journey is often fragmented across institutions, accounts and products, where the average consumer has five to seven financial accounts, according to research from American Banker with insights provided by Mastercard, where I lead open finance and developer experience. This leaves financial providers with blind spots, as they lack a complete view of each customer.

Open finance has made it possible to close that visibility gap at a scale that didn’t exist even a few years ago, by connecting permissioned financial data across accounts, payment rails and financial relationships, and then turning it into intelligent insights institutions can use, while giving consumers greater visibility and control over how their financial information is shared. ​

That enriched, contextualized data—spending velocity, merchant patterns, recurring payments, income flows—is precisely what fraud models need, too. Traditional fraud systems relied heavily on static identity attributes: a Social Security number, a date of birth, a billing address.

As bad actors have become more sophisticated by using AI to manufacture synthetic identities and automate account takeovers, static signals are increasingly unreliable. This is particularly challenging during digital account opening, when a synthetic identity may appear to be a legitimate applicant with a thin credit history.

One in ten financial institutions experienced more than 10,000 fraud attempts in 2024 alone, according to Alloy, spanning synthetic identities, account takeovers and credential theft. As these threats evolve, institutions need to look beyond traditional verification methods and consider a broader range of signals when assessing identity and risk.

What’s harder to fake is a complete financial life: the cadence of a weekly grocery run, the pattern of a direct deposit every other Friday or the way someone pays their rent, tops off their transit card and sends money to a family member. These behavioral fingerprints are extraordinarily difficult for a fraudster to replicate, and they’re the exact same signals institutions use to personalize offers and deepen engagement. ​

This convergence matters because most institutions are resource-constrained.

The American Banker research cited above shows that only 8% of banks and credit unions have the data maturity to support personalization at scale. At the same time, according to KPMG, 89% of banking executives are increasing their budgets to address cyber risks. These investments are often made in parallel—separate teams, separate budgets, separate technology stacks—when the underlying data problem is largely the same.

Institutions that recognize this can build once and benefit twice. A data enrichment capability that standardizes raw transaction streams into clean merchant labels, categories and behavioral indicators doesn’t just power a personalized savings recommendation—it also makes anomalous behavior easier to spot.

A consumer whose spending patterns suddenly shift from routine grocery purchases to high-value electronics at unfamiliar merchants looks different against a well-understood behavioral baseline. Without that baseline, the same transaction might not raise a fraud flag at all.

The business case reinforces this dual logic. According to Mastercard research published in partnership with FT Longitude, 60% of organizations adopting open finance have already developed the ability to generate real-time AI insights about risk and consumer engagement—not one or the other, but both from the same data foundation. And 57% have used those same capabilities to strengthen their security and fraud protocols.​

Of course, using the same data for personalization and fraud defense raises the stakes on responsible governance.

Consumers are increasingly willing to share their financial data, but that willingness is conditional. Nearly half say it depends on understanding how their data will be used and what they’ll get in return. If institutions leverage behavioral data to improve someone’s banking experience and protect them from fraud, that’s a value exchange most consumers can embrace and that sets a stronger foundation of ongoing trust with their provider. If the governance isn’t clear, the trust erodes quickly.

Executives should look to embed security by design in all data projects—not as an afterthought, but as a foundational principle. Responsible data governance isn’t a constraint on innovation; it’s the precondition for it.

The institutions that get this right will be the ones that earn ongoing consent, which fuels better data, which drives both better personalized experiences and stronger defenses. It’s a flywheel in which consumers recognize the value and remain in control, while providers use increased data sharing to drive continuous innovation loops, with trust at the heart of what keeps it turning. ​

The financial services industry tends to silo innovation. Customer experience teams pursue personalization; risk teams pursue fraud prevention; data teams try to serve both and end up building twice.

The more productive frame is to recognize that personalization and fraud defense are two expressions of the same underlying capability: knowing your consumer well enough to serve them—and protect them—in real time.

That is the broader opportunity of open finance, and institutions that build their data foundations with both outcomes in mind won’t just deliver better experiences or catch more fraud. They’ll do both more efficiently, and while earning greater trust and building long-lasting relationships with the people they serve.

#3172. Robinhood Made $173 Million From Prediction Markets Last Quarter, More Than From Crypto. Can That Carry the Stock?

Prediction markets have quickly become one of Robinhood's most important sales drivers.

Robinhood Markets (HOOD -10.32%) reported its third-quarter results after the market closed on Oct. 27, and performance in the period didn't thrill investors. The company reported non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share of $0.51 on sales of $1.42 billion, missing the average analyst estimate of earnings per share of $0.56 on sales of $1.43 billion. While the company's revenue was up 12% year over year to a new record high, earnings per share fell 3% from the prior-year period.

The market wasn't thrilled with the quarterly print, but there were some bright spots. Notably, sales from the company's prediction market ventures increased more than sixfold annually to reach $173 million. The big growth helped offset a substantial decline for the company's cryptocurrency segment, which saw sales decline 55% year over year to reach $120 million. Are event contracts now central to Robinhood's growth story?

The rise of prediction markets has occurred at an incredible pace, with service providers including Kalshi and Polymarket rapidly growing their user bases and commanding billion-dollar market capitalizations. Event contracts allow investors to bet on real-world outcomes in spheres including politics, awards show results, sports, and even the weather -- and participants can sell in and out of positions based on current market rates in much the same way that they would buy and sell stocks.

The popularity of prediction markets is exploding, and Robinhood's massive category revenue growth reflects how lucrative it can be to provide services in this category. Given the expansion trajectory for the company's event contracts segment, Robinhood's prediction market business looks poised to achieve an annual revenue run rate of more than $1 billion in the near future -- and it could still have room for big growth from there.

With the company's cryptocurrency segment seeing big sales declines, strong performance for the event contracts business is helping to smooth out performance and facilitate continued overall revenue growth for the overall business. On the other hand, there are still some significant risks associated with the rapidly ascendant prediction-market business.

The prediction market industry is still in its "Wild West" phase, and there's a real possibility the category will face a wave of new regulations in the not-too-distant future. Shifting regulatory dynamics could cause growth in the category to slow substantially or introduce higher expenses for operators, and there's even a risk that current operators of event contracts and adjacent services could wind up being hit with sizable fines at some point down the road.

Given recent trends in financialization, regulators may have trouble getting the toothpaste back in the tube with prediction markets -- but investors should understand that disruption risks exist for Robinhood's hot new business category. While the introduction of Robinhood's event-contracts business has been an undeniable boon to sales and earnings and could help carry the stock over the long term, there's still some uncertainty on that front.

#3170. Bluetooth 7 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“Imagine a smartwatch that syncs hours’ worth of sensor-rich training data to your phone in seconds, smart glasses that deliver richer AI experiences by offloading data for processing, or a smart home product that completes a firmware update with virtually no user-visible downtime,” Øyvind Strøm, executive vice president of the short-range business unit at Nordic Semiconductor, said in a statement. “Bluetooth HDT paves the way for more sophisticated, data-intensive Bluetooth applications.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

All we know about which specific devices will get the technology first is that it will start with wireless audio.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

#3169. Human Accountability: How Construction Leaders Can Scale AI Ethically

Steve Cangiano is the Chief Product Officer at CMiC, a global leader in construction management software.

​By now, many construction firms have tried to incorporate AI into their operations; however, fewer use it daily.

As a marketing leader at a construction ERP software company, I’ve watched a familiar pattern emerge across the industry: A firm loads every corporate document into a database, uses a chatbot to get responses to questions and expects results to follow. While some employees find value in that process, most are not there yet.

The gap between pilot and practice is rarely about technology. It is about how AI is introduced, where it is applied and whether people trust what it produces. Here is what I have learned about closing that gap.

In recent years, the most common mistake I see is companies deploying AI without identifying the problem they’re trying to solve or the goal they’re trying to achieve. General-purpose tools ask users to discover their own use cases, and most busy professionals will not take the time to do so.

Instead, start with dedicated agents built for the tasks people already perform manually. These are often routine job-cost and project-accounting activities that consume hours each week. Some examples include importing a long spreadsheet of customer records, simulating how an accounting batch will affect the general ledger before posting it or previewing the impact of a transaction on a project budget. When an agent performs these tasks reliably, adoption often follows because the value is obvious. Dedicated agents can also help newer employees complete tasks in screens they have never used or cannot remember how to find.

What follows is scalability. Once teams understand what standard agents can do, they can start asking better questions or entering better prompts. For example, they may ask, “I have a problem nobody anticipated. Can I build an agent for that?” Giving teams the tools to customize or create their own agents can turn early familiarity into organization-wide use.

At the highest level, leaders often measure AI returns in larger areas or functions, such as cost control or schedule performance. While those gains matter, the most immediate return comes from something simpler: the speed at which the business can answer its own questions.

By design, the answers users are looking for have always lived in the ERP system. What has been missing is access. For some firms, especially those without large IT or analytics teams, an executive who wants to know which regions deliver the highest margins on a specific project type has to request a custom report, which can take a week or more to prepare.

Query agents can change that. A leader can ask in plain language, “What is our margin on tilt-up concrete jobs in Texas?” They can then get an answer in moments. Field teams benefit in the same way when they need a detail buried in a spec book or drawing.

Meanwhile, task agents that create and update records may deliver a quieter return. Each automated task takes a little less time and effort. Over the first 12 to 24 months, that reduced friction adds up, particularly in project accounting and cost control, because people are more willing to complete work that takes less effort.

Historically, construction has been known for slow technology adoption, but things are changing. Here is how I look at it: Working with AI is a skill, much like learning Excel or another application. Prompting an agent resembles giving instructions to a colleague, and many people are not used to articulating requests that way. The learning curve is short, but it is real.

This is where proper design comes in. Rather than sending users to a separate chat tool, embed the agent directly in the screens where work already happens. When the agent appears in a side panel, users can keep their context and work alongside it.

Another barrier to adoption is trust. From what I’ve seen, most users will let an agent take them about 80% of the way through a process and then want to verify the result themselves. That instinct is natural. Every action an agent takes should link directly to the record it created or changed, so a user can review it in one click before finalizing or posting the update. In time, each verified result can build confidence, which, in turn, can drive adoption.

With seasoned employees heading into retirement, many executives are counting on AI to preserve the knowledge those workers take with them. The way I see it, AI will not replace that experience or take over every construction workflow anytime soon. Instead, it will give employees the chance to elevate their performance.

There is a caveat, though. While professionals may use agents to manage volume, they will still need to apply judgment and creativity where it matters. That makes human accountability essential.

Consider a common scenario: concrete yield on a job. An AI system might flag that output per labor hour has declined over the past two weeks, but an alert is not a decision. A project leader still needs to review the data, confirm the trend and determine the cause. The value here lies in flagging the issue earlier than anyone would have noticed otherwise.

This is also the case in software development. Engineers who use AI to write code remain accountable for the code they submit. Construction teams should hold AI-assisted work to the same standard as fully human work.

For leaders ready to invest in AI, the model is simple. Begin with practical tasks your teams already perform, design for trust from day one and keep people accountable for outcomes.

It is critical to remember that a trust-but-verify approach is not a limitation. Rather, it is the foundation for making AI a part of your day-to-day operations.​​
